title: LiLiCorr: Lightweight Likelihood Correlation of Parallel Drafts for Speculative Decoding
author: Matan Rusanovsky et al
topic: speculative decoding, parallel drafts, dflash, diffusion drafter, likelihood correlation
description: This paper asks how a block-parallel drafter for speculative decoding can produce jointly coherent drafts without extra drafter passes or pushing reranking work onto the target model. DFlash drafts a block of B = 16 tokens in one pass, with slot 0 as the anchor and 15 speculative slots, but it trains on per-slot marginals, so each token is plausible alone while the block may be incoherent. LiLiCorr keeps the drafter's top K = 8 candidates at each slot and turns each into a node that sums the frozen target embedding of the token, the drafter's hidden state, an MLP over five confidence scalars, and learned slot and rank embeddings. A two-layer bidirectional Transformer with slot-distance attention biases runs over this lattice, fuses in the target's hidden state, and emits a unit-normalized out vector and in vector per node. Adjacent slots are scored by a scaled cosine between a node's out vector and the next node's in vector, with scale 8. Training uses a local softmax over candidates given the previous token, supervised along the oracle prefix, plus a penalty on probability placed on candidates the target ranks below the ground truth. The drafter is co-trained with this loss through the log-probabilities and hidden states, with candidate indices held fixed. At decoding, one network pass yields all vectors, a greedy left-to-right walk commits one token per slot, and the target verifies the block in a single pass, accepting a prefix. Because only adjacent-pair scores over K candidates are formed, the V^B joint is never materialized.

title: DiffusionGemma Technical Report
author: DiffusionGemma Team et al
topic: dlm, diffusion llm, open-weight, moe, sampler distillation, rl
description: This paper asks how to get an open model that generates text far faster than token-by-token decoding without giving up reasoning, multimodality, and long context. DiffusionGemma warm-starts from the post-trained Gemma 4 26B A4B mixture-of-experts model and keeps the same backbone, using it as a causal encoder that builds a KV cache of the prompt and past text, and as a bidirectional decoder that cross-attends to that cache. Text is produced block-autoregressively: a 256-token canvas starts as uniformly random tokens and is refined by multinomial (uniform-noise) discrete diffusion, so any token can still be revised within the canvas. Each step also feeds back a self-conditioning signal, made by passing the previous predicted distributions through the embedding matrix and a small feedforward block. The default sampler is entropy-bounded: it commits the lowest-entropy positions up to an entropy budget and re-noises the rest, anneals temperature from 0.8 to 0.4, and stops early once predictions are confident and stable. Finished canvases are encoded and appended to the cache. Training has two stages. Supervised fine-tuning noises each canvas at a random level, uses block-diagonal attention, and minimizes cross-entropy on the clean tokens. Then online sampler distillation plus reinforcement learning has the model act as its own teacher, generating high-step trajectories scored by rewards, to raise quality and compress denoising into few steps. It reaches about 20 tokens per forward pass.

title: Physics of Language Models: Part 4.1, Architecture Design and the Magic of Canon Layers
author: Zeyuan Allen-Zhu
topic: architecture, canon layers, synthetic pretraining, linear attention, reasoning
description: This paper asks which architectural differences between language models are real and which are noise, since academic-scale pretraining on real data is too noisy to tell. It builds controlled synthetic pretraining tasks, each isolating one capability: Depo (reasoning depth, finding the k-th successor in a permutation of directed edges without chain-of-thought), Brevo (reasoning breadth, listing all vertices reachable in a dependency graph in topological order), Capo (knowledge capacity, measured in bits per parameter on synthetic biographies), Mano (knowledge manipulation, mentally evaluating modular arithmetic over stored facts), and Lano (hierarchical structure, inferring context-free grammar parses). Models are trained across several data scales and sizes with identical data. Within this setup the author proposes Canon layers, a lightweight way to add horizontal information flow between neighboring tokens. A Canon layer is a trainable causal 1-D convolution with kernel size 4, using element-wise weights over the current and three preceding positions, zero-padded at the start, with no nonlinearity, and added back through a residual connection (h' = h + conv(h_t, ..., h_{t-3})). It can be inserted at four places in a block: A before attention after the norm, B inside attention on the concatenated Q/K/V projections, C before the MLP after the norm, and D inside the MLP before the activation. The same layer is added to Transformers, linear attention (GLA), and Mamba2-style SSMs, whose built-in convolution acts as a partial Canon-B. It helps because it gives a cheap local path that attention would otherwise have to spend capacity on, and it speeds up learning of deep multi-hop skills, with gains appearing mostly at greater depth.

title: Scaling Latent Reasoning via Looped Language Models
author: Rui-Jie Zhu et al
topic: looped language models, latent reasoning, pretraining, adaptive depth, ouro
description: This paper asks whether looped language models (LoopLM) can reach frontier-level parameter efficiency at scale by building latent reasoning into pre-training instead of relying on chain-of-thought text. The model is a decoder-only transformer (RoPE, SwiGLU, sandwich RMSNorm) whose stack of layers, 24 for the 1.4B model and 48 for the 2.6B model, is applied repeatedly with tied weights. Four recurrent steps are used in most training, after an initial 8-step phase that was unstable. After every step the same LM head produces a prediction, and a parallel exit gate outputs a per-step exit probability. These probabilities form a distribution over exit steps. Stage I trains the model on the expected next-token loss under that distribution, plus an entropy bonus. This is equivalent to a KL term against a uniform prior over steps, so the gate does not collapse onto the deepest step. The weight on this term (beta) is lowered from 0.1 to 0.05. Stage II freezes the LM and trains only the gate, using a binary cross-entropy target built from how much each extra loop actually reduces the loss. Pre-training covers 7.7T open-source tokens: web data, then annealing on math and code, long-context training, and mid-training on SFT-style data. The 2.6B model is made by duplicating the 24 layers. Reasoning SFT follows. At inference, the model exits at the first step where the cumulative exit probability passes a threshold. During decoding, the KV cache from only the last step, or an average over steps, can be reused, cutting memory 4x, though prefilling still needs a separate cache per step. The authors attribute the gains to better knowledge manipulation rather than more stored knowledge.

title: Clover: Regressive Lightweight Speculative Decoding with Sequential Knowledge
author: Bin Xiao et al
topic: speculative decoding, parallel decoding, medusa, regressive connection, attention decoder
description: This paper asks how to make speculative decoding both cheap and accurate when the draft heads that guess several future tokens, as in Medusa, predict each token independently and so ignore the sequential dependence of language. Clover keeps the target LLM frozen and attaches a small set of draft heads, three in the paper, that share the target's LM head. Its Regressive Connection feeds each head the embedding of the token the previous head speculated. That embedding is the one-hot token vector multiplied by the transposed, normalized LM head weights, which the authors argue sits closer to last-layer hidden states than an embedding-table lookup. The Attention Decoder is the regressive unit. It is a cross-attention block whose query comes from the normalized previous hidden state and whose key and value come from the previous speculated token's embedding. It adds its output residually to that hidden state, and the result goes to the head's MLP to predict the next token. It handles only two vectors per request or beam, so overhead is negligible, and it beat a plain MLP in the authors' tests. An Augmenting Block, an extra transformer block appended to the target model and initialized from its last block, enriches the hidden states for the first head. Its attention sub-block gives most of the gain, at about 1/N_layer of the inference time. Each head proposes top candidates. Conditioning on earlier guesses lets Clover use a smaller, more informative token tree than Medusa's Cartesian-product tree, merged by prefix and checked in one target forward pass using tree attention, with the tree size fixed at 4 for large-batch serving. Only the new modules are trained, with AdamW and a cosine schedule.

title: PSD: Pushing the Pareto Frontier of Diffusion LLMs via Parallel Speculative Decoding
author: Shengyin Sun et al
topic: dlm, speculative decoding, parallel decoding, training-free, hierarchical acceptance
description: This paper asks how to accelerate diffusion language models along two axes at once: spatially, by unmasking several tokens per denoising step, and temporally, by collapsing several future denoising steps into one verification call. Each alone saturates, since aggressive parallel unmasking forces low-confidence tokens to commit and degrades quality, while existing speculative methods still reveal only one token per step and are capped by acceptance. The proposed Parallel Speculative Decoding (PSD) is training-free and policy-agnostic. From a single forward pass, it applies any configurable parallel unmasking policy to reveal multiple positions, then builds speculative drafts at multiple depths by filling the remaining masked positions in descending confidence order, with no extra model calls. A final batched verification pass applies hierarchical acceptance, keeping the deepest draft whose speculated tokens still agree with the verifier's updated predictions, which stops errors from aggressive unmasking from propagating. This works because the set of high-confidence masked positions tends to stay stable as denoising proceeds, so today's confidence ranking is a good guess for the next few steps. On Dream-7B, LLaDA-1.5, and openPangu-7B-Diffusion across GSM8K, HumanEval, and MBPP, PSD reaches 3x to 5.5x tokens per forward pass while staying within 1 point of greedy accuracy in most settings. For example, on GSM8K with LLaDA-1.5 it doubles Spiffy's 2.0x to 4.0x tokens per step, while LoPA pushed to 4.9x collapses HumanEval pass@1 to 23.8%, compared with PSD at 4.2x and no loss. Speculative depth beyond about 3 adds little, and the authors note that evaluation is limited to math and code, so effects on open-ended generation remain untested.

title: Multi-Token Residual Prediction
author: Yufeng Xu et al
topic: dlm, residual prediction, speculative decoding, remasking, multi-token decoding
description: This paper asks whether a diffusion language model can decode several tokens per step while keeping the dependencies between them, instead of sliding along the usual threshold-controlled trade-off where quality drops as more tokens are revealed at once. Its key observation is that the backbone's logits at adjacent denoising steps are very similar when only a few tokens are unmasked between them, so the residual between steps is far smaller than the logits themselves and a much easier prediction target. The proposed Multi-token Residual Prediction (MRP) attaches a lightweight 3-layer transformer to a frozen backbone that predicts this inter-step logit residual from the backbone's hidden states. A chain of MRP steps then approximates what extra backbone passes would produce, decoding more tokens from a single backbone forward through the shared LM head, and it is trained by distillation on still-masked positions. MRP is used in three ways: as a drafter for lossless speculative decoding, whose proposals the backbone verifies jointly in its next forward; as direct decoding without verification for a tunable speed-quality trade-off; and, under low-threshold dynamic decoding, as a remasking scheme that revokes over-eager reveals that the corrected logits do not confirm. Implemented in SGLang on SDAR-Chat 1.7B, 4B, and 8B, speculative mode gives 1.17x to 1.40x lossless speedup (largest on 8B GSM8K), and direct mode at K=1 runs 1.43x to 1.61x faster with close accuracy (90.1 vs 90.9 on 8B GSM8K). Remasking at threshold 0.5 recovers at least 11 points on every task and scale, up to 22.6 on HumanEval and 17.7 on GSM8K, while keeping roughly 0.76x to 0.88x of dynamic decoding's throughput on reasoning tasks, and its gains fade toward zero at high thresholds where the backbone is already conservative.

title: On the SPOT: Enhancing Speculative Decoding for Diffusion Language Models via Commit-Order Prediction
author: Eliezer Shlomi et al
topic: dlm, speculative decoding, commit order, draft trees, gumbel coupling, lossless acceleration
description: This paper asks how to bring lossless speculative decoding to diffusion language models, where bidirectional attention inside a block means the target decides not only what token to write but also where to write it next, so a drafter must predict a trajectory of block states rather than a fixed sequence of tokens. Its key finding is that the tokens are largely known in advance: the target's stale predictions from the previous pass already match the eventually committed token at 92% to 100% of positions, while which position commits next is the hard part. The proposed SPOT is a 0.62M-parameter drafter that reads only the target's output distributions and, after each hypothetical commit, predicts the next position, growing a tree of candidate block states ordered by prefix probability. The target then checks every drafted state in a single batched forward and accepts the longest prefix that matches its own trajectory. To keep this exact when sampling, coupled-noise verification shares per-position Gumbel noise between drafter and target, which makes the target's choice deterministic given the noise so state equality can verify the whole tree at any temperature while still recovering the target distribution. A variant, SPOT-Sets, extends this to dynamic threshold decoding by drafting whole commit sets along with their tokens. On SDAR-8B, SPOT cuts target passes by up to 6.8x and reaches up to 3.4x the throughput of standard decoding, uses 16% to 36% fewer target forwards than Spiffy's calibrated draft graph, and transfers across six diffusion models, including LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B, without retraining. SPOT-Sets adds 59% average throughput over the threshold decoder alone. The authors note that gains shrink when verification is costly (as with wide blocks) or acceptance is low, and that SPOT-Sets needs a short calibration for each new target.

title: Transformers Learn Shortcuts to Automata
author: Bingbin Liu et al
topic: transformers, automata, circuit complexity, krohn-rhodes, algorithmic reasoning, length generalization
description: This paper asks how shallow, non-recurrent Transformers manage algorithmic reasoning that seems to require many sequential steps, studying the question through semiautomata, which update a finite state with each input symbol. It defines a shortcut as a network that exactly simulates an automaton on length-T inputs with o(T) depth, and shows that instead of representing states and iterating the transition one step per layer, a Transformer can represent and hierarchically compose the transition functions themselves. Via divide-and-conquer composition, every semiautomaton has an O(log T)-depth shortcut with width polynomial in the number of states. Using the Krohn-Rhodes decomposition, which factors any solvable semiautomaton into modular counters and resettable memory units joined by a cascade product, solvable automata even get constant-depth shortcuts, since soft attention computes prefix sums and hard attention finds the most recent reset. A depth-2 construction handles gridworlds through a nearest-boundary detector, and conversely, constant-depth shortcuts for non-solvable automata such as those generating A5 would imply TC0 = NC1. Empirically, GPT-2-style Transformers trained on 19 automata with T = 100 reach over 99% in-distribution accuracy on all of them (best of 20 runs), with non-abelian groups needing more depth, for example S5 rising from 51.8% at 8 layers to 97.2% at 12, and learned attention heads matching the boundary-detector construction. These shortcuts are brittle, though: training is unstable, accuracy drops under distribution shift and on longer sequences because the model learns intermediate quantities like counts rather than the state, and LSTMs stay perfect where Transformers fail. Scratchpad training with a recency bias steers Transformers back toward recurrent solutions that generalize.

title: LED: Improving Masked Diffusion Language Models by Lookahead Editing
author: Yuyan Zhou et al
topic: dlm, masked diffusion, uniform diffusion, token editing, lookahead decoding, expressivity
description: This paper asks whether masked diffusion language models can gain the expressivity of iterative token revision without giving up the simple, easy-to-optimize transition schedule that makes them easier to train than uniform diffusion models. The authors first argue theoretically that masked models have a zero schedule-matching loss and admit larger learning rates, but because committed tokens can never be rewritten they stay within TC0, whereas uniform models, which can repeatedly rewrite tokens, reach NC1 at the cost of harder optimization. The proposed Lookahead Editing (LED) adds a rewritable proposal branch alongside the usual clean and masked branches. During training, a pretrained masked diffusion model generates proposals containing both correct and incorrect tokens, and LED is trained with plain cross-entropy to keep good proposal tokens and fix bad ones, using an attention mask in which each mask and proposal block attend bidirectionally to each other and to preceding clean blocks. At inference, before each real decoding step LED runs K lookahead passes that repeatedly rewrite a draft of future tokens, then commits high-confidence tokens to the masked sequence, where they become fixed as in standard masked diffusion. This works because revision happens only in the temporary proposal while the committed sequence keeps the mask-based schedule. Fine-tuned from Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen3-8B, LED raises the eight-benchmark average over matched MDM SFT from 45.4 to 56.8 and from 60.8 to 68.5, and LED-8B with SFT alone (68.5) edges out LLaDA2.1-16B (67.9), which uses continued pre-training, SFT, and RL, with gains such as AIME 2025 rising from 23.3 to 40.0. Lookahead trades speed for accuracy, with LED-8B on AIME 2025 ranging from 40.0 at 16 tokens/s to 33.3 at 44 tokens/s, and K = 2 works best, since longer lookaheads tend to accumulate bad proposals and hurt accuracy.

title: CPU-ARC: Agentic Reasoning Caching for on-CPU Reasoning Reuse
author: Peter Belcak et al
topic: agentic reasoning caching, reasoning reuse, semantic functions, small language models, cost reduction
description: This paper asks whether the reasoning a large language model uses to solve a class of problems can be turned into a reusable, executable cache that a small model can run cheaply without losing correctness or robustness. Its method, agentic reasoning caching, has a builder model analyze a source model's reasoning transcript and construct a cache entry: a network of Python semantic functions that refer to inputs and sub-functions by natural-language descriptions rather than fixed names. The builder works through five phases (input-output isolation, decomposition, parameter recognition, planning, and implementation), and each candidate function is tested against the transcript's answer and rewritten on failure. At inference time a new query is matched to a cache entry by embedding similarity, a small target model extracts the parameters, and plain CPU code executes the reasoning, so the expensive reasoning becomes a one-time build cost while the small model only handles extraction and classification. Across MATH-500, AIME '24/'25/'26, GPQA Diamond, GSM8K, MMLU-Pro, and SciBench, cache accuracy matched or exceeded the source model on seven of eight benchmarks (for example AIME '25 rose from 83.3 to 93.3), while per-sample invocation was 16x to 291x cheaper. The caches also proved robust to perturbation, solving roughly 91% to 99% of reworded or re-parameterized versions of problems they already handled.

title: LoopAhead: Speculating Ahead for Faster Decoding in Looped Language Models
author: Zixuan Liu et al
topic: looped language models, speculative decoding, decoding latency, lookahead drafting
description: This paper asks how to speed up generation in looped Transformers, which reuse the same layers over several recurrent depths and therefore pay repeated weight-access and sequential cost for every token. It proposes LoopAhead, a lossless speculative decoding framework in which a lightweight lookahead drafter (a two-layer Transformer with hidden size 512) reads early-loop hidden states and proposes several future tokens at once instead of waiting for the model to reach full depth. Intermediate-loop readouts act as cheap feedback that suspends candidate branches conflicting with deeper predictions and resumes them later, so less compute is wasted on wrong speculative paths, while only the full-depth model makes the final accept and prune decisions. This works because early-loop predictions already agree strongly with full-depth outputs under the same prefix, and that agreement rises quickly across loops, so early drafts are often correct and wrong ones can be caught early. Under greedy decoding on Ouro and Raven looped models across GSM8K, MATH500, HumanEval, MBPP, and BBH, LoopAhead reaches 2.82x to 7.82x speedups over autoregressive decoding, for example 4.27x on GSM8K for Ouro-1.4B versus 2.92x for LoopSpec and up to 7.82x on HumanEval for Raven-TinyLlama. Greedy outputs exactly reproduce autoregressive outputs, and sampling uses standard speculative acceptance against the full-depth distribution, so quality is preserved.

title: RangeSWA: Training-Free Length Extrapolation for Continuous Diffusion Language Models
author: Guangfu Guo et al
topic: dlm, continuous diffusion, length extrapolation, sliding-window attention, training-free
description: This paper asks how to let continuous diffusion language models generate text far beyond their training length without collapsing into repetition, semantic drift, and quality loss. The proposed RangeSWA requires no parameter updates and combines local sliding-window attention with coarse summaries of distant token blocks and content-based retrieval of relevant distant blocks, all within a single softmax. It also remaps distant positions back into the trained positional range, and applies a correction to attention from control tokens to body tokens, since sliding windows otherwise shift too much attention toward those control tokens. A denoising-stage-adaptive window uses a wider local window at high noise and narrows it as denoising proceeds, matching the shift from global layout to local detail. On ELF-B/M/L checkpoints at 8k tokens, RangeSWA reaches GPT-2 Large generative perplexity of 18.37 / 32.13 / 33.39 versus 153.55 / 165.93 / 118.31 for plain sliding-window attention, while full attention degenerates badly (42.6% four-gram repetition on ELF-B). The authors caution that low perplexity can hide repetition, noting that on ELF-B RangeSWA raises repetition relative to SWA, and they show the method transfers to CoLa and LangFlow with large reductions in repetition.

title: Measured Coupling for Parallel Decoding in Diffusion Language Models
author: Tal Oved et al
topic: dlm, parallel decoding, mean-field decoding, token coupling, training-free
description: This paper asks which masked tokens a diffusion language model can safely commit together in a single denoising step, since tokens predicted independently can combine into incoherent pairs. It replaces the similarity-based pairwise penalty used in training-free mean-field parallel decoding with a measured coupling, defined as how much committing token j changes the log-margin confidence at position i, which captures both conflict and mutual support. These couplings are estimated by cheap block-local probes run inside the same forward pass as the main step while reusing the KV cache, and they plug directly into the existing mean-field update with no training or auxiliary model. The approach works because it identifies positions that confirm each other so they can be committed together, and ablations that shuffle the couplings or replace them with a uniform support bonus lose the gain. On LLaDA-8B-Instruct at a matched threshold, the method needs 24% to 43% fewer steps than mean-field decoding, for example 40.1 versus 65.4 NFE on GSM8K at nearly identical accuracy (76.27 vs 76.57). Averaged over three models and four benchmarks the accuracy cost is about 1.1 points, though the drop is larger on Dream, and wall-clock throughput improves in most settings including with a KV cache.

title: Self-Distilled Reasoner: On-Policy Self-Distillation for Large Language Models
author: Siyan Zhou et al
topic: distillation, llm
description: On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) introduces a training framework in which a single large language model serves as both teacher and student by conditioning on different information. The teacher receives privileged information, such as ground-truth answers or reference reasoning traces, while the student receives only the original problem and generates its own on-policy trajectories. Training minimizes the per-token divergence between the teacher and student probability distributions along the student-generated trajectories, providing dense supervision without requiring an external teacher model or reward model. The method additionally introduces per-token pointwise KL clipping to prevent stylistic tokens from dominating the learning signal and improve training stability. Experiments on Qwen3 models across AIME 2024, AIME 2025, and HMMT 2025 demonstrate that OPSD consistently outperforms supervised fine-tuning and matches or exceeds GRPO while requiring substantially fewer generated tokens and training steps. Ablation studies show that forward KL, a thinking-mode-on teacher paired with a thinking-mode-off student, and full-vocabulary logit distillation provide particularly effective training configurations.

title: Elastic-dLLM: Position Preserving Context Compression and Augmentation of Diffusion LLMs
author: Junyi Wu et al
topic: dlm, mask tokens, rope, context compression, iterative folding
description: The paper asks whether the large computational cost in diffusion language models comes from repeatedly processing many future [MASK] tokens that contribute little new information, and how to reduce this redundancy without breaking generation. It shows that although [MASK] tokens have highly redundant feature representations and mostly interact locally with each other, they encode critical structural signals through their RoPE positional indices, especially for determining where content should be generated and when to terminate. Based on this, the method compresses the future [MASK] context by sparsely sampling tokens from each block while keeping decoded history, the current block, and the terminal region dense, and crucially preserves each retained token’s original RoPE coordinate so that positional priors remain unchanged. This design works because generation in dLLMs is strongly guided by positional encoding rather than token identity for masked positions, so maintaining the positional “skeleton” preserves semantics even under heavy token reduction. The framework further extends to iterative folding, where older decoded tokens are also sparsified under the same positional-preserving rule for long-context scaling, and to block dLLMs by adding a single protected [MASK] token at the final RoPE position to explicitly reintroduce the terminal signal that guides EOS prediction.

title: Looped Diffusion Language Models
author: Sanghyun Lee et al
topic: masked diffusion, looped transformers, test-time compute, language modeling, training efficiency
description: This paper asks whether looping layers, a trick from autoregressive looped transformers, helps masked diffusion language models (MDMs), which already iterate across denoising steps. The proposed LoopMDM splits the denoising transformer into a head, a mid-block and a tail. The head and tail run once, while the mid-block, a small stack of early-middle layers (layers 1 and 2 of a 12-layer model), has shared weights and is applied S times, so the effective depth grows without adding parameters. Training minimizes the standard MDM NELBO on the final loop output while sampling the loop count S uniformly from 1 to Smax at each step, which makes representations stable for any S at inference, even beyond Smax. Training FLOPs are matched to the baseline by using fewer steps. Ablations show that looping a few early-middle layers works best, while looping many layers or using a very large Smax hurts. On a 170M model, LoopMDM matches baseline test NLL with up to 3.3x fewer FLOPs on LM1B, OpenWebText and FineWeb-Edu, and improves perplexity and downstream accuracy. On GSM8K it gains up to 8.5 points and beats a deeper 21-layer baseline with similar per-step FLOPs. Analyses with Sudoku under a fixed left-to-right order and rising mask-to-mask attention suggest masked positions act as a workspace that loops refine. Gains peak at intermediate noise levels, so stopping when the hidden-state change falls below 0.1 cuts the average loop count from 12 to about 5.

title: Learning Generalized Gumbel-max Causal Mechanisms
author: Guy Lorberbom et al
topic: counterfactual reasoning, structural causal models, gumbel-max, couplings, variance reduction
description: This paper asks how one should choose a causal mechanism for counterfactual reasoning when interventional data cannot identify it. Prior work on Gumbel-max structural causal models picks the Gumbel-max trick because it is counterfactually stable. The authors instead treat the choice as an optimization problem, for example minimizing the variance of an estimated counterfactual treatment effect. They show that any mechanism defines an implicit coupling between interventional distributions that share exogenous noise. They prove that Gumbel-max couplings are not maximal couplings, though they are within a factor of two of maximal, and that no fixed implicit coupling can be maximal for every pair of distributions over three outcomes. They then propose two learnable families, called gadgets, that contain Gumbel-max as a special case. Gadget 1 learns an auxiliary joint distribution over outcomes and a latent variable and transposes the Gumbel noise for one sample. Gadget 2 draws a latent cluster z, and a neural network produces a nonnegative matrix that is Sinkhorn-normalized and corrected with an accept-reject step, so marginals are exactly correct for every input distribution. Training relaxes the argmax to a softmax and minimizes a loss over a distribution of query pairs. Experiments show near-maximal couplings when the training distribution is focused, lower variance than Gumbel-max under non-monotonic rewards, and lower treatment-effect variance in a sepsis simulator, including on held-out queries.

title: An Identifiability Theory of Masked Prediction: Mode Blindness and Mask Schedules
author: Yichao Cai et al
topic: masked prediction, identifiability, mask schedules, mode blindness, masked diffusion, theory
description: This paper asks when a small excess risk in masked prediction guarantees recovery of the true joint distribution. The authors work on finite product spaces with masked-block log loss, where model conditionals come from a single joint distribution, and define an epsilon-identifiability modulus, the worst-case total-variation error among joint distributions whose excess risk is at most epsilon. The central finding is mode blindness. If data have two well-separated modes and every mask in the schedule leaves enough visible context to pin down the mode, then a model with the wrong mode weights can have exponentially small excess risk, so a constant error persists. An information decomposition explains this: the masked loss only sees mode-weight mismatch where the visible context leaves the mode uncertain. Excess risk is bounded above and below by the mode-weight KL times the schedule-averaged residual mode uncertainty, which is the expected posterior variance of the mode indicator. Assigning schedule mass to low-visibility masks gives an explicit recovery bound that scales like the square root of epsilon over that mass. Positive full-mask probability is necessary and sufficient for distribution-free control of joint KL by excess risk. Exact calculations and gradient descent experiments confirm these predictions, and exploratory natural-text measurements for code versus prose and German versus English show uncertainty falling with visible context.

title: How to Train a Swarm
author: General Reasoning team
topic: agent swarms, multi-agent reinforcement learning, collective inference-time scaling, latency pressure, communication
description: This post asks how to train agent swarms with reinforcement learning so that they scale useful parallel work, which it calls collective inference-time scaling. It starts from the reasoning paradigm, noting that models only learned to think longer because the RL setup rewarded it, and that choices such as GAE lambda below 1 can collapse response length. For swarms, nothing in a task reward favors parallel work, so the setup must make faster work pay. The authors describe their RLCR recipe, which uses a shared policy and a flat collective advantage for all agents. They compare two sources of latency pressure. An explicit latency penalty subtracts a scaled wall-clock term from the task reward, but it interacts with other quantities and is sensitive to the time limit. A time limit instead caps wall-clock time and takes the return so far, which requires environments with anytime-return measures such as tests passed. Their Avalon-M1 model raises the cap from 2 hours to just over 5 hours during training. Communication primitives should stay simple, such as direct messages and shared message boards. They track signs of life: larger collectives do more useful work, nearly twice the average by step 200, communication intensity rises, and collectives reach comparable scores sooner, with a single agent needing 4x as long at matched tokens. Open problems include small training collectives versus large deployed ones, coarse credit assignment, and shared environments.

title: TTRL: Test-Time Reinforcement Learning
author: Yuxin Zuo et al
topic: test-time training, reinforcement learning, majority voting, reasoning, unlabeled data
description: This paper asks how a language model can run reinforcement learning on unlabeled test data when there is no ground-truth reward available at inference time. The answer is Test-Time Reinforcement Learning (TTRL), which borrows a common test-time scaling trick, majority voting, to manufacture rewards. For each prompt the policy samples many responses (64 rollouts in the experiments), an answer extractor pulls out the predicted answers, and the most frequent answer is treated as an estimated label. Each rollout then receives a rule-based reward of 1 if its answer matches that consensus and 0 otherwise, and the policy is updated online with GRPO (a down-sampled 32 responses per prompt are used for training, with a cosine learning rate peaking at 5e-7). The method works even though the pseudo-labels are often wrong, for three reasons the authors analyze. Rewards are denser than labels, so a wrong consensus label still correctly penalizes the many scattered wrong answers (a Lucky Hit effect); on AIME 2024 label accuracy was only about 37% while reward accuracy reached about 92%. RL is also fairly tolerant of reward noise. And because training is online, the model improves and then produces better voting labels. Results are large: Qwen2.5-Math-7B improves pass@1 on AIME 2024 from 12.9 to 40.2 (about 211%), averaging a 76% gain across AIME, AMC, MATH-500 and GPQA, with gains on LLaMA, Mistral and DeepSeek models and on reasoning models. TTRL even exceeds the initial model's maj@n ceiling and approaches RL trained directly on test labels. It can fail when hyperparameters are poor or when the model lacks prior knowledge of hard problems.

title: Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights
author: Rikiya Takehi et al
topic: weight-space programming, interpretability, llm agents, weight editing, neural network weights
description: This post asks whether a general-purpose frontier LLM, used as is and without gradients or training loops, can read neural network weights to understand what they do and write or edit weights to change behavior, much as a programmer reads and edits code. The authors call this concept Weight-Space Programming and stress it is a statement about an emerging capability, not a proposed method. Using a model they call GPT-6 Astra, they run eight experiments. On reading: given 17,253 raw MLP weights with no tools it names which of four games the PPO network was trained on, infers what a diffusion model draws, and from only the middle transformer blocks of tiny character-level models it identifies the training language and finds every induction (copying) head; it could not spot a sycophantic Gemma 3 270M from weights alone, but succeeded when allowed to inspect attention patterns. On writing: one-shot edits of 3.5% of weights fix a Kinetix car policy stuck in a local minimum (success in all 1,024 episodes), and weights written from scratch for three MinAtar games beat PPO trained for 100 million steps, while a 1.5M-parameter Go network with 50 forward passes beats an equal-sized PPO net. Finally, on Qwen3.5-0.8B it traced reasoning loops to one direction written by MLPs in layers 15 and 19, subtracted it from 131,072 weights (0.016%), and raised MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and IFEval from 21.0% to 62.3%. It could not improve a model that did not loop, showing edits remove obstacles rather than add abilities.

title: LLM Neuroanatomy II: Modern LLM Hacking and hints of a Universal Language?
author: David Noel Ng
topic: layer duplication, relayering, transformer circuits, qwen, model hacking, interpretability
description: This post asks whether RYS (Repeat Your Self), the trick of duplicating a block of middle transformer layers with no weight changes and no training, was a fluke of Qwen2-72B or a general property of transformers. Testing on Qwen3.5-27B, the author first shows the anatomy directly: cosine similarity of hidden states for English and Chinese facts and poems reveals an encoding phase in the first few layers, a broad reasoning phase (roughly layers 10 to 50) where content matters more than language, and a decoding phase at the end. The duplicable layers are the reasoning region, since a format-agnostic space tolerates looping back. A full scan of duplicated blocks (i, j) scored on small math and EQ probes found the best single block, layers 24 to 35, adds 11 layers (+17%) for a combined delta of +0.2104, while a tight block at 29 to 34 does nearly as well for less. Single-layer repeats can help math (layer 10 repeated three times) but are unstable. A beam search with 3,024 measured candidates and an XGBoost surrogate that ranked 2 million configurations (Spearman 0.93 on holdout) found stronger but costlier composed configurations, with sublinear gains. After re-measuring 397 candidates on larger Math120 and EQ140 sets, the Pareto frontier contained only contiguous mid-stack blocks, such as repeating layer 33 alone for +1.56% size, so the author released RYS-Qwen3.5-27B S, M, L and XL models, concluding that discrete reasoning circuits are general.

title: DUET: Optimize Token-Budget Allocation for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
author: Haoyu Hu et al
topic: rlvr, grpo, token budget, rollout allocation, efficient training, reasoning
description: This paper asks how to cut the token cost of reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), where rollout generation dominates compute, without losing accuracy. Prior work controls only one lever, either which prompts get rollouts or how long each rollout runs; DUET (DUal-controlled tokEn allocaTion) controls both under one shared token budget as a thin layer over GRPO. In the Allocate phase, a cost-weighted Neyman rule sets each prompt's rollout count to its informativeness divided by the square root of the Lagrange multiplier times its mean length; informativeness is estimated online from the running standard deviation of advantage-weighted log-probabilities, and the multiplier is found by bisection each step and acts as the budget-pressure signal. In the Generate phase, a marker-gated abort stops a rollout shortly after a parsable answer appears and aborts marker-less rollouts past an adaptive quantile length threshold, but continues them with probability epsilon and reweights by 1/epsilon so the gradient stays unbiased. The Update phase uses the importance-corrected, masked clipped loss. Overhead is under 1% per step. On Qwen3-1.7B-base trained on MATH, DUET beats GRPO, DAPO, ARRoL and VIP on MATH-500, GSM8K, AIME-24 and HumanEval (for example MATH-500 61.6 versus 56.8 for GRPO) with a 1.62x speedup, and at half the budget it still beats them all with a 2.51x speedup. Results hold from Qwen3-4B to 14B and on Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, and the advantage widens as the budget tightens because the allocator concentrates on harder prompts.

title: Budget Internalization: Fixed-Budget RLVR Trades Test-Time Scaling for In-Budget Accuracy
author: Ilia Zavidnyi et al
topic: rlvr, test-time scaling, grpo, reasoning budget, truncation
description: This paper asks what happens to a reasoning model's ability to benefit from extra test-time tokens when it is trained with RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR) under a fixed rollout cap. The authors run GRPO on Qwen3.5-4B, Gemma4-E2B and Nemotron-3-Nano-4B using DeepScaleR math data (and Reasoning Gym tasks), with caps of 4k or 8k tokens for Qwen and 1k or 2k for Gemma and Nemotron, giving zero reward to rollouts that are truncated without an answer. They find a crossover they call budget internalization: accuracy on AIME beats the base model near the training cap but then saturates, and falls below the base at larger budgets. For Qwen 4k training the change is +34.8 points at 4K but -30.2 points at 64K, and trained models rarely use extra tokens (mean 4.97k versus 27.32k for the base at 64k). The effect transfers to GPQA-Diamond and LiveCodeBench, where it often just shortens outputs with small accuracy loss. Budget forcing helps the base model, but forcing the trained model to continue with Wait does not restore scaling. Ablations show that scoring of truncated rollouts, training data difficulty (GSM8K preserves more scaling) and KL anchoring matter most, while Dr.GRPO normalization does not. SFT on artificially truncated traces reproduces the effect, whereas SFT on naturally short traces does not, so the cause is length-censored training signal rather than RL itself. No intervention keeps both the in-budget gain and base-model scaling.

title: Learning to Imagine: Integrating Counterfactual Thinking in Neural Discrete Reasoning
author: Moxin Li et al
topic: counterfactual thinking, hypothetical question answering, neural discrete reasoning, tabular and text qa, numerical reasoning
description: This paper asks why neural discrete reasoning (NDR) models fail on hypothetical questions such as what a ratio would be if revenue were doubled, and how to give them counterfactual thinking. The authors show that TAGOP, the state-of-the-art model on TAT-QA, drops from 68.6 to 3.8 F1 when a related assumption is added to the question. They propose a Learning to Imagine (L2I) module that builds a counterfactual context from the factual context and assumption in two steps: a tagging head identifies the fact to intervene on, and a deriving head picks one of eight discrete operators (SWAP, ADD, MINUS, MULTIPLY, DIVISION, PERCENT INC, PERCENT DEC, SWAP MIN NUM) and tags the premise in the assumption, so the assumed value replaces the target fact precisely. A RoBERTa encoder feeds a matching block of three shared-parameter cross-attention layers (with self-attention) linking the factual part and the assumption, and the module is trained with extra cross-entropy losses on tagging and operator choice on top of the QA loss. The authors also build TAT-HQA, 8,283 hypothetical questions annotated by finance students. TAGOP-L2I reaches 54.4 EM and 54.7 F1, about 19.8 percent over the best baseline, beating a contrastive-learning variant (45.4 EM). Operator selection reaches 96.4 percent accuracy and target fact picking 82.9 percent. Explicit operators and separate imagination work because they make the intervention precise, unlike generating text or learning it implicitly.

title: Adaptive Test-Time Compute Allocation for Block Diffusion Language Models in Complex Reasoning
author: Yi Lu et al
topic: block diffusion, diffusion language models, test-time compute, adaptive decoding, long chain-of-thought
description: This paper asks how block diffusion language models (BDLMs) should allocate test-time compute in long chain-of-thought reasoning, where faster parallel decoding usually costs accuracy. The authors add adaptivity at two levels. Bounded Adaptive Confidence Decoding (BACD) replaces a fixed unmasking threshold with the running mean confidence of previously decoded tokens, clipped between a lower bound (0.7) and an upper bound (0.9), so easy spans decode aggressively while uncertain ones stay cautious, and the highest-confidence token is unmasked if none passes. Think Coarse, Critic Fine (TCCF) generates the exploratory reasoning with a large block size (16) and, after replacing the end-of-thinking marker with a prompt to check for mistakes, switches to a small block size (4) for verification and the final answer. To train for large blocks they use Progressive Block Size Extension, raising the SFT block size from 4 to 64 in stages, which beats direct training at block size 16 by 6.7 accuracy points. They adapt Qwen3-8B-base into TDAR-8B. On six benchmarks, BACD cuts function evaluations 7.7 percent versus fixed-threshold decoding, and with TCCF the model reaches 49.5 percent average accuracy, +3.4 points over TraDo-8B-Thinking, with a 2.38x NFE speedup. It also helps a 30B model (70.1 percent). It works because reasoning is heterogeneous: exploration tolerates coarse parallel decoding, but verification needs fine granularity.

title: PrefixFlow: Training-Time KV Caching for Schedule-Level Prefix Reuse in LLM RL Training
author: Pengbo Li et al
topic: rl training systems, kv caching, prefix reuse, grpo, distributed training
description: This paper asks how to avoid recomputing the shared prompt prefix N times when RL post-training turns one prompt into N rollouts, a cost that dominates in long-context RAG, video and chart workloads where prefixes are 76 to 99 percent of tokens. Prior designs reuse the prefix inside one computation graph, packed sequence or kernel, and their savings often fail to become shorter steps under memory limits and parallelism. PrefixFlow moves reuse into the training schedule with a training-time KV cache. Phase A runs one prefix forward and caches per-layer keys and values; Phase B trains suffixes as ordinary microbatches that read the cached K/V and write back only gradients gK/gV; Phase C runs one delayed prefix backward on the accumulated gradients. This is correct because the only interface between suffix and prefix graphs is K/V and gK/gV, and prefix backward is linear in incoming adjoints (prefix-gradient superposition). Dormant prefix activations are offloaded to pinned host memory during Phase B, freeing HBM; context, pipeline and data parallelism each use a local scheduling rule, tensor and expert parallelism need no change, and MoE works under Rollout Routing Replay. Implemented on TorchTitan, it matches full-sequence training within BF16 tolerance and speeds up end-to-end verl RL training by 1.90x (6.1x on the actor update), reaches 4.4x at an 83 percent prefix ratio, and cuts Phase-B peak HBM by up to 59 percent.

title: Trajectory-Level Speculative Decoding for Diffusion Language Models
author: Tianxiang Pan et al
topic: diffusion language models, speculative decoding, parallel decoding, inference acceleration, tree verification
description: This paper asks how to speed up diffusion language models (dLLMs) when parallel decoding collapses to one token per step under low confidence, and why autoregressive speculative decoding cannot simply be transplanted. The authors observe that in Fast-dLLM, such low-confidence degeneration occurs in over 80% of steps, even though the correct token usually sits in the top-3 candidates. Because a dLLM draft must specify positions and unmasking order, not just token identities, they speculate over denoising trajectories. High-confidence tokens (above threshold tau) form a root block; low-confidence positions seed a tree of draft blocks, using top-k expansion at the root and top-1 expansion deeper, so cost grows as O(W times D) rather than exponentially. All draft blocks are verified in one forward pass with a blockwise attention mask: each block attends bidirectionally to cached prefix and suffix but not to sibling blocks. Inter-block speculation also drafts block t+1 jointly with block t when its early confidence is high. A theorem shows exact equivalence to Fast-dLLM under top-1 decoding with cached KV and no inter-block speculation; deviations arise as trajectory drift from added parallelism. On LLaDA-7B and Dream-7B, steps fall 30-40%, tokens per step rise from 2.6 to 4.3, with 7-14x speedup over vanilla dLLMs, 1.3x over Fast-dLLM, and under 1% accuracy change. It works because verification reuses the forward pass and the roofline leaves spare compute for extra draft blocks.

title: Fast at the Frontier, Wrong at the Fallback: A Commit-Level Analysis of Threshold Decoding in Diffusion Language Models
author: Roman Makarov et al
topic: diffusion language models, threshold decoding, frontier, early EOS, decoding policy, commit order
description: This paper asks where the speed and the errors of confidence-threshold decoding in diffusion language models actually come from. Open-weight DLMs commit every masked position whose confidence passes a threshold (0.9), fall back to the single most confident position when none does, and never revise commits. The authors trace every commit of four models (Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion 3B and 8B, LLaDA-8B, Fast-dLLM v2 7B) on math, code, translation and summarization, recording distance from the frontier, the leftmost masked position. Most tokens become confident only near the frontier (15-24% only once they are the frontier, 60-64% within seven positions), so a policy committing only at the frontier has at least 0.92 times the tokens per forward pass of vanilla across 34 settings. The accuracy loss in wide windows comes from commit order, not parallelism: committing one token per step changes accuracy by at most two points, while frontier order gains 3 to 46 points on GSM8K. The worst case is an early end-of-sequence token that cuts the answer short. Fallback commits are 11-35% of commits but start 61-72% of failures that left-to-right decoding avoids, and replaying a failure with only that step changed repairs it more often than changing a matched earlier step. Committing only at the frontier recovers most lost accuracy on all four models.

title: Mask-Aware Policy Gradients for Diffusion Language Models
author: Haran Raajesh et al
topic: diffusion language models, reinforcement learning, policy gradient, unmasking order, masked diffusion, reasoning
description: This paper asks how to apply policy-gradient reinforcement learning to masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) when the log-likelihood is intractable and existing methods model only token predictions while ignoring the order in which positions are unmasked. The authors formalize each denoising step as a two-stage action: predict tokens at masked positions, then choose which positions to keep unmasked and which to remask. The trajectory likelihood then factorizes into a token term and a position term, and the policy gradient splits into a token gradient and an unmasking gradient. To make the position term differentiable, greedy top-K remasking is replaced by probabilistic remasking: K positions are sampled without replacement from a Plackett-Luce distribution proportional to exp(v/tau) of the model's own token log-likelihoods, so no extra parameters or forward passes are needed. They use the StepMerge approximation (N=32 segments, K=12 sampled boundaries) with GSPO, LoRA and LLaDA-8B-Instruct, and prove with a minimal counterexample that a token-only gradient can be zero along a direction that improves expected reward. Results reach 87.1% on GSM8K and 53.4% on MBPP, with consistent gains of 2 to 4 points over the token-only StepMerge baseline, GDPO and SPG. Gains grow with block size, since more masked positions make order matter more, and it also reaches SPG's final accuracy faster in wall-clock time.

title: FEROM: Frontier Endogenous Reveal-Order Marginal Policy Optimization for Masked Diffusion LMs
author: Zian Su et al
topic: masked diffusion language models, reinforcement learning, reveal order, Rao-Blackwellization, GRPO, policy optimization
description: This paper asks how to estimate the policy gradient for masked diffusion language models when the order in which positions are revealed is itself computed from the model's own logits, making it an endogenous latent variable with an enormous discrete space. Sequence-level rewards see only the finished response, so a trajectory-level estimator that follows one sampled reveal path attributes reward to order randomness the reward never observes. FEROM instead targets the rollout-induced marginal response policy and derives a Rao-Blackwellized identity (Fisher's identity) showing the marginal gradient has covariance no larger than the trajectory gradient. It writes the marginal score as a sum over edges of a reveal-state DAG weighted by posterior edge occupancy. Since exact occupancies are combinatorial, Frontier Reveal Marginalization keeps a frontier of high-mass partial states, computes local reveal probabilities exactly from confidence-score CDFs without extra forwards, scores several tokens per forward with macro reveals, and branches to cover alternative orders under a fixed state-evaluation budget. FEROM-GRPO then uses a detached token-score surrogate. On LLaDA-8B-Instruct at 256 tokens, it leads compared small-budget baselines on MATH-500 (43.9) and HumanEval (46.3) and ranks second on GSM8K (85.7), trailing on MBPP. Offline studies show better marginal-gradient alignment with larger budgets, and differentiating the reveal-order term destabilized training.
